screens.body:
'Shift left' means moving security earlier: catch flaws in design and code review, not after launch. A bug found in a design doc costs nearly nothing; the same bug exploited in production costs customers.

Practical shift-left: a 2-minute threat model per feature ('what could go wrong here?'), security checks in code review, and scanners in your pipeline. Small habits, huge savings.

options: Catch flaws early in design/code, not after launch
Move servers to the left coast
check.question: Shift left means…

screens.heading: Find it early, fix it cheap
screens.keyPoint: A design-doc fix beats a breach every time.

screens.body:
Code review is your cheapest security tool. A reviewer checklist: is input validated server-side? Any secrets in the diff? Auth checks on new endpoints? Dependencies added — are they healthy?

Reviewers catch what scanners can't: logic flaws, like a refund endpoint that never checks the purchase exists. Automate the easy stuff; human-review the thinking.

options: Validation, secrets, auth checks, new dependencies
check.question: A security code review checks…

screens.heading: Review with a security eye
screens.keyPoint: Humans catch logic flaws; scanners catch patterns.

screens.body:
Automated scanning runs in CI on every push: SAST scans your source code for risky patterns, DAST attacks your running app like an outsider, and dependency scanners flag known-vulnerable packages.

They're noisy — false positives happen — but they're tireless. A scanner that cries wolf ten times and catches one real SQL injection still earned its place.

options: SAST scans code, DAST attacks the running app, dependency scans flag bad packages
check.question: Automated security scanners:

screens.heading: Robots that hunt bugs

screens.body:
Penetration testing is hiring professionals to break into your system — with permission, on a schedule, with a defined scope. They think like attackers so you can fix like defenders.

It's not a substitute for the basics: pen-test a house with no locks and you'll just get an expensive list of open doors. Harden first, pen-test to verify.

options: Authorized experts attack your system so you can fix first
check.question: Penetration testing is…

screens.heading: Friendly attackers, on purpose
screens.keyPoint: Harden first, then pay pros to verify.

screens.body:
Bug bounties pay independent researchers for reporting vulnerabilities instead of exploiting them. It's a standing invitation: 'find our flaws, we'll pay and fix.'

For a student or startup, the takeaway isn't running a bounty — it's the mindset: assume flaws exist, make reporting easy (a security contact email), and thank reporters instead of threatening them.

options: Rewarding researchers who report flaws responsibly
check.question: Bug bounties:

screens.heading: Pay for flaws, not breaches

screens.body:
Incidents WILL happen. Incident response is your plan: detect (alerts, logs), contain (isolate the affected part), eradicate + recover (fix, restore from clean backups), then learn (blameless postmortem).

Write the plan BEFORE you need it — including who gets called at 3 AM. In a crisis, you follow the checklist; you don't invent one.

options: Detect → contain → recover → learn, from a pre-written plan
check.question: Incident response:

screens.heading: When it happens: the plan

screens.body:
AppSec as a habit: threat-model each feature (2 minutes), review diffs with the checklist, keep scanners green, update dependencies monthly, and rehearse your incident plan yearly.

Security isn't a phase — it's how you work. The devs who internalize this become the ones teams trust with the important systems.

options: Daily habits: model, review, scan, update, rehearse
check.question: AppSec done right is…

screens.heading: Security as a habit

screens.body: OWASP Testing Guide (owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide). OWASP SAMM (owaspsamm.org). NIST SP 800-61 incident handling guide (nist.gov).
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: SAMM tells you how mature your process is.
